assessment_policy.certificate: Completion certificate requires verified enrolment and completion of learning components

questions.question: What is the direct energy source used by muscles for movement?
options: Lactate
ATP (adenosine triphosphate)
Oxygen alone
Phosphocreatine alone
questions.explanation: ATP is the immediate energy source. Phosphocreatine, glycolysis and oxidative metabolism help regenerate it.

questions.question: Which description best matches the ATP–PCr pathway in swimming?
options: It is particularly important during short explosive starts and breakouts
It is the only pathway used for the entire 1500 m race
It begins working only after 30 seconds
It replaces the need for recovery
questions.explanation: The phosphagen pathway supports rapid ATP regeneration in short, explosive efforts; other pathways also contribute.

questions.question: AthlyraX uses LP and LT to describe which relationship?
options: Two completely separate energy systems
LP means low pace and LT means long training
Different training emphases associated with glycolytic work
Two names for aerobic EN1
questions.explanation: LP and LT are coaching categories for different demands, not separate biochemical energy systems.

questions.question: Which statement about lactate is supported by Part 1?
options: Any lactate means a swimmer has trained incorrectly
Lactate can be produced and used as fuel; its level alone does not diagnose fatigue
Lactate is always a harmful waste product
A lactate value tells us the exact reason for a slower swim
questions.explanation: Part 1 explains that lactate is not simply waste, and an isolated measurement does not establish a cause of fatigue.

questions.question: A swimmer reports 8/10 perceived effort. What does this tell us?
options: Their blood lactate is exactly 8 mmol/L
Only the anaerobic system was active
The swimmer felt the effort was very demanding
Their stroke technique must have failed
questions.explanation: RPE describes perceived demand; it is not a lactate reading or a precise energy-system diagnosis.

questions.question: What should a coach conclude if breathing appears comfortable again after a short rest?
options: The swimmer is fully recovered for every task
Breathing is one clue, but the next effort and movement quality still matter
Phosphocreatine must be 100% restored
The swimmer should immediately sprint maximally
questions.explanation: Breathing recovery is useful but does not guarantee restored speed, technical control or overall readiness.

questions.question: A swimmer completes the same 100 m time on two different days, but rates one effort 5/10 and the other 8/10. What is the best interpretation?
options: Both efforts had identical internal demand
The second day proves the athlete has lost aerobic fitness
The swimmer must have changed energy systems
The same performance can be experienced differently; consider context
questions.explanation: A matching stopwatch result does not imply matching experience. Sleep, training load, pacing and technique may help explain the difference.

questions.question: Which set of observations gives a broader poolside picture than swim time alone?
options: Breathing, perceived effort, repeatability and movement quality
Only the number of metres completed
Only the swimmer’s age and body mass
Only the name of the planned energy zone
questions.explanation: Part 2 identifies these four complementary observations while emphasising that none proves a diagnosis by itself.

questions.question: A swimmer’s four fast 25 m times are 14.8, 15.0, 15.6 and 16.1 seconds. Which claim is justified?
options: The swimmer definitely has poor aerobic fitness
Lactate alone caused the decline
Performance became slower across the repetitions
The phosphagen pathway stopped working
questions.explanation: The decline is observed. Its cause requires additional information about recovery, pacing and movement quality.

questions.question: What extra information would be useful when interpreting that declining 25 m series?
options: Only the swimmer’s personal best from last year
Actual rest, start and breakout quality, stroke rhythm and effort
The coach’s preferred energy-zone label
The total number of swimmers in the pool
questions.explanation: Part 3 highlights these measurements and observations to examine plausible explanations.

questions.question: A swimmer holds approximately 1:30 for six 100 m repetitions while RPE rises from 4 to 8. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: The external times are stable but the experienced demand appears to increase
The set has become objectively easier
Each repetition must have exactly the same physiological cost
The athlete has proven a particular blood-lactate level
questions.explanation: Stable times do not necessarily mean stable internal demand; RPE contributes context.

questions.question: Two swimmers both complete 100 m in 1:30. One rates the effort 5/10 and the other 9/10. What does the example show?
options: The swimmers necessarily have the same capacity
The second swimmer must be unwilling to train
Both swimmers experienced identical effort
A shared time need not represent an equal relative challenge
questions.explanation: The external result is the same, but the swimmers report very different demands.

questions.question: After 60 seconds of rest, breathing settles but the next effort is slower with poorer movement. What is the best conclusion?
options: The next performance suggests readiness was not fully restored for that task
Breathing recovery guarantees peak speed
The swimmer was not trying
The stopwatch must be broken
questions.explanation: Visible breathing recovery does not guarantee the same performance or technical quality on the next task.

questions.question: Which sequence matches the evidence-based approach in Part 3?
options: Assign an energy system, ignore feedback, increase metres
Record the observation, consider alternative explanations, decide what to check next
Assume a biochemical cause, then select a training zone
Wait for a race personal best before noting any response
questions.explanation: Part 3 explicitly separates observation, possible interpretation and the next useful measurement.

questions.question: Which statement about the three energy pathways is accurate?
options: Each pathway switches on only when the previous one switches off
Glycolysis is the only source of ATP in hard swimming
The pathways overlap, while their relative contributions vary with demand
Only aerobic metabolism contributes during swimming
questions.explanation: Part 1 explains that phosphagen, glycolytic and oxidative pathways all contribute, with varying emphasis.

questions.question: A coach tells a swimmer that a slower second sprint proves a precise biochemical deficiency. Why is this unsupported?
options: All swim times are unreliable
Sprint performance is unaffected by recovery
Breathing patterns can establish all biochemical causes
A change in time alone does not establish the cause; other evidence is needed
questions.explanation: Part 3 distinguishes measurable outcomes from possible—but unproven—physiological explanations.

questions.question: Which basic training record best reflects Part 3?
options: Swim time, actual recovery, effort rating and a movement observation
Total distance and an assumed lactate score only
Planned send-off without achieved swim time
A subjective judgement of the swimmer’s attitude only
questions.explanation: The recommended simple record combines external performance, actual recovery, subjective effort and observed movement.

questions.question: What is an appropriate way to respond when a swimmer reports high effort?
options: Treat high RPE as poor attitude
Listen to the swimmer, consider performance and context, and avoid unsupported labels
Conclude that one specific energy pathway has failed
Ignore the report whenever the swim time is fast
questions.explanation: The three parts emphasise individual experience, open questions and appropriately cautious interpretation.
